title: CRT Explicit Construction: Non-Coprime Bézout Formula (OQ-04-OQ-03-OQ-01)
description: Makes the non-coprime CRT solution construction explicit: for x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) with gcd(m,n)|a-b, the explicit solution is x = a − m·(gcdA(m,n)·q). Generalizes to list of congruences by induction. 8 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Chinese Remainder Theorem (Sunzi, ~3rd century CE) in its classical form requires coprime moduli. The general non-coprime case has a compatibility condition and explicit solution via Bézout coefficients.
overview.problemStatement: Make the non-coprime CRT solution explicit: for compatible congruences, give a formula in terms of Bézout coefficients.
overview.proofStrategy: Two congruences: x = a − m·(gcdA(m,n)·q) where gcd(m,n)·q = a−b. Verify x ≡ a (mod m) and x ≡ b (mod n). List case: induction, at each step compute new LCM and apply 2-case formula.
keyInsights: **Bézout formula**: if gcd(m,n)·s + m·t = 1 (Bézout), then x = a + m·(-t·((a-b)/gcd)) solves both congruences explicitly.
**LCM propagation**: after solving two congruences modulo lcm(m,n), new congruences reduce to the 2-case applied to (lcm, m_next, a, b_next).
**Euclidean domain generality**: the formula works over any Euclidean domain R, not just ℤ.

sections.title: Explicit Bézout CRT Solution Formula
sections.summary: crtSolve₂: explicit 2-moduli formula. crtSolve₂_congruence₁, _congruence₂ verification. crtSolveList: list case by induction.
sections.mathContext: $x = a - m \cdot (\text{gcdA}(m,n) \cdot q)$ solves $x \equiv a \pmod{m}$, $x \equiv b \pmod{n}$.

conclusion.summary: 8 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Explicit non-coprime CRT formula proved over Euclidean domains.
conclusion.implications: The explicit formula enables efficient CRT reconstruction in cryptographic applications without requiring coprime moduli.
openQuestions: Can the explicit formula be extended to the general case of Dedekind domains?
Can the Chinese Remainder Theorem be proved for non-principal ideal domains?
Can the formula be used to prove correctness of RSA with shared prime factors?
